scenes.visual: Keep the title Copy First, Then Divide. Briefly show skin repair and an onion root as context, then bring a model cell forward.

scenes.tts: A cell copies its D N A before mitosis, so each new cell can get a full set of instructions. Copy first, then share the copies. Picture two groups that each need a whole recipe book. Tearing a book in half gives each group only half the recipes. Copying it first gives each a full book. The comparison breaks because a cell does not decide anything. Proteins copy and share the D N A. In interphase, G one is growth, S phase is D N A copying, and G two is preparation for division. Each copied chromosome has two identical sister chromatids, joined at the centromere.

scenes.visual: Lead with DNA copying and the complete-set outcome. Compare a book torn in half with a copied book given to each group; label this an analogy and transition to proteins doing the copying. Show G1, S and G2 under interphase. Track color-coded model chromosomes, doubling each into sister chromatids at S phase; label the centromere. Do not show chromatids separating yet.

scenes.tts: Mitosis shares the copied chromosomes between two nuclei. Spindle fibers are thin protein fibers that attach to chromosomes and move them. In prophase, chromosomes coil up. Near the end, the nuclear envelope breaks down. In metaphase, spindle fibers line the chromosomes up across the middle. In anaphase, sister chromatids separate and move to opposite ends. In telophase, a full set reaches each end. A new nuclear envelope forms around each set.

scenes.visual: Continue with the same copied chromosomes. Label prophase, metaphase, anaphase and telophase as the envelope breaks down late in prophase, chromosomes align, sister chromatids separate, and two envelopes form. Keep chromosome colors consistent so a complete matching set can be followed into each nucleus. Spindle fibers attach and move chromosomes; do not animate DNA copying during mitosis.

scenes.tts: Cytokinesis divides the cytoplasm, making two cells. It often starts as mitosis is ending. In an animal cell, a ring pinches the membrane inward. The furrow deepens until the cell splits. A plant cell has a stiff wall and cannot pinch. A cell plate forms across the middle and grows outward into a new wall. The two new cells usually have the same D N A.

scenes.visual: Begin the animal furrow during late mitosis, then complete the split. Beside it, show a plant cell plate forming centrally and growing outward into a separating wall. Label mitosis as nuclear division and cytokinesis as cytoplasmic division. Show each daughter with the same complete chromosome set.

scenes.tts: These new cells let living things grow, repair damage and replace cells. Skin cells divide behind a wound to replace cells that were lost. Near an onion root tip, cells divide. Behind that zone, the new cells stretch, pushing the root through the soil. For a single-celled amoeba or yeast cell, division can make a new organism.

scenes.visual: Place this scene after cytokinesis. Show skin cells dividing behind a wound, then an onion root with distinct division and elongation zones. Show division and stretching contributing to root growth. Finish with a single-celled amoeba dividing as an example of asexual reproduction; remove the old opening question boxes.

scenes.tts: A smaller point is why cells stay small. Oxygen, food and wastes cross the membrane. In a cube model, as a cell gets bigger, its volume grows faster than its surface. It has less membrane for each bit inside. Real cells are not cubes. Cells also control their size, so surface area is one limit among several.

scenes.visual: Use one short closing scene labelled A smaller point: cell size. Compare small and large model cubes with membrane-crossing arrows. Emphasize surface versus inside without the old arithmetic table. Label the cubes as a geometry model, then show varied cell shapes and the caveat that surface area is one limit among several.
Keep the silent end card with the film title Copy First, Then Divide.
